texto:
Adorn Cosmetics, a Melbourne skincare company that turned over six million dollars a year at its peak according to 7NEWS, is set to close after a move to an Adobe e-commerce platform that its founder, Briony Kennedy, says cut sales by about 30% as soon as the new website went live. The account comes from a 7NEWS Australia report published on YouTube on November 8, 2026, under the title "Cosmetics empire crumbles after Adobe website disaster." In it, Kennedy says the roughly one million dollars a year the company spent on Instagram and Facebook advertising was sending people to links that no longer led back to the store. Adobe declined to comment for legal reasons, and the report says a mediation attempt between the parties has failed.
In Short
A Melbourne cosmetics founder told 7NEWS that moving her online store to Adobe's e-commerce platform cut sales by about 30% and left the company's paid social ads pointing nowhere, and the report says the business is about to close. The story matters to any brand that spends heavily on ads, because those ads only pay off if the website they send people to keeps working through a platform change. It is one side's account: Adobe would not comment, mediation failed, and the report does not explain what the agency that built the site did or what exactly broke.
What 7NEWS reported
The report runs for less than three minutes. It opens by casting the dispute in stark terms: "A Melbourne mother is locked in a David and Goliath battle with an American software giant she says has destroyed her cosmetics company." The narration continues: "The multi-million dollar business was decimated after a computer upgrade backfired."
Adorn, as the report describes it, is an award-winning Australian brand that sells sustainable skincare to "thousands of mature aged women." A line in the transcript sets out its packaging approach: "We use biodegradable, refillable, recyclable products." According to 7NEWS, the company at its peak was "turning over six million dollars a year." The report does not name the currency, the year of that peak or whether the figure refers to revenue from the website alone.
The central claim is put in the narrator's voice. Adorn, 7NEWS says, "is drowning in debt after software giant Adobe convinced Bryony to switch from her basic free website to an expensive online store or e-commerce platform." Kennedy explains her motives in two short sentences: "I just wanted to make sure our security was fine. It was going to improve sales." The report adds that Adobe was "quoting revenue increases of between 34 and 94 percent," and names the firm that carried out the work: "Pairing with local agency Convert Digital to implement the change."
What followed, in Kennedy's telling, went wrong from the start. "Absolutely nothing went right but I wasn't allowed to get out of the contract that I was in," she says. Then comes the number at the centre of the story: "When the site actually launched, our sales dropped instantly by about 30 odd percent."
According to 7NEWS, Kennedy laid off staff and sold her family home "to try to save the ailing company," before abandoning the Adobe website and starting again on Shopify. "But it's too late," the narrator says, adding that Kennedy, riddled with debt, faces bankruptcy. Her own words are brief: "I've really, really tried. And there's nothing more that I can do."
There is also a personal note that the report leaves in. "I know I'm not a failure but you can't help but feel like I should have known better," Kennedy says.
Adobe's side is a single sentence. "A spokesperson from Adobe headquarters in the United States told Seven News they will not comment on this case for legal reasons," the report states. It then adds: "A mediation attempt between the parties has failed." The final line of the transcript before the reporter's sign-off reads: "Barring a miracle, Adorn Cosmetics will close tomorrow." The segment is credited to reporter Jackie Quist.
On YouTube, the video had 943,317 views, 6,301 likes and 2,401 comments by November 9, 2026. The channel, 7NEWS Australia, has 2.27 million subscribers. The video's description summarises the case in one sentence: "Melbourne cosmetics entrepreneur Briony Kennedy has faced bankruptcy after her $6 million sustainable skincare company Adorn Cosmetics collapsed following a failed website migration to Adobe's e-commerce platform."
The ads that stopped leading anywhere
For performance marketers, the most specific detail in the report concerns paid social. "Advertising we were paying for on Instagram, Facebook, about a million dollars a year," Kennedy says. "All of those ads that we were paying for were not linking back to the website."
By PPC Land's calculation, one million dollars a year is about a sixth of the six million dollars Adorn turned over at its peak. The report does not say whether the two figures refer to the same year, so the ratio is an approximation rather than a measured share of revenue.
What "not linking back" meant in practice is not explained. Ads can lose their destination in several ways during a platform change: product and category addresses can change while the ads still point to the old ones, catalogue feeds connected to ad accounts can carry outdated links, or tracking can break so that clicks still arrive but sales are no longer recorded against the campaigns. The report does not say which of these, if any, occurred, how long the problem lasted or who was responsible for fixing it.
The mechanics of keeping old links alive are well documented. When an address changes, a 301 redirect tells browsers and crawlers that the page has moved permanently, so that visitors and ad clicks reach the new location. Google updated its site move guide in June 2026 to cover www and non-www domain variants; the guide says permanent redirects do not lose PageRank and recommends keeping them in place for at least a year. Technical changes that look minor can carry measurable costs. An SEO agency's client lost 20% of its traffic after applying lazy loading to every image, even though its PageSpeed score rose from 65 to 92. Shopify's own data, published in April 2026, associated every 100 milliseconds of slower loading with a conversion rate about 3.5% lower, a correlation rather than a controlled test.
None of this establishes what happened to Adorn's site. It does show why a 30% fall in sales after a relaunch, if accurate, would not be an unusual pattern for a storefront whose traffic depends on paid links and on pages behaving as they did before the switch.
What the 2021 announcements said
The report gives no dates for the switch, but public material from the time does. On September 29, 2021, the Australian trade publication B&T reported that Adorn was upgrading to Adobe Commerce. According to that article, Adorn had used an open-source version of Magento since its launch in 2009. Adobe agreed to acquire Magento for $1.68 billion in May 2018, so the "basic free website" described by 7NEWS appears to have been the free, open-source edition of a platform that Adobe already owned, and the upgrade a move to its paid commercial product.
Adobe published its own case study of the project on its Australian business blog, under the title "Adorn Cosmetics gives its e-commerce experience a makeover with Adobe Commerce." The page carries no date. According to Adobe, the upgrade would replace four separate software packages with the Adobe Commerce dashboard and reporting tools, and would support personalised product recommendations. In the case study, Kennedy is quoted as expecting that faster product pages and simpler analytics would lift sales and save her team time. B&T quoted Scott Rigby, whom it described as Adobe's head of digital transformation for enterprise solutions in Asia Pacific, as saying Adorn was well on its way to realising its e-commerce ambitions.
The two pages also show how much the brand relied on social channels. Adobe's case study put Adorn's following at nearly 75,000 on Facebook and 20,000 on Instagram, while B&T cited almost 100,000 social media followers in total.
Neither page names an implementation partner, a launch date for the new site or a projected revenue increase. The 34% to 94% range cited by 7NEWS does not appear in either. A separate study listed on Adobe's Australian site with a December 2021 date, carried out by IDC and sponsored by Adobe, put the gain at 29% higher platform revenue for companies invested in Adobe Commerce. That is not the figure in the report, and the report does not say where its range came from.
What the report does not establish
Several facts that would matter in any assessment of responsibility are absent from the broadcast.
The timeline is the first gap. The report gives no date for the contract, for the launch of the Adobe site or for the move to Shopify. The 2021 announcements suggest the project began about five years before the broadcast, but how long the Adobe site ran, and when sales fell, is not stated.
Convert Digital's role is the second. 7NEWS names the Melbourne agency as the partner that implemented the change, but says nothing about the scope of its work, whether it built and maintained the site, whether it was party to the contract Kennedy says she could not leave, or whether it was asked for comment. Commerce platforms are commonly deployed by a systems integrator that designs the build, migrates the data and tests the result, which is where questions about redirects, feeds and tracking would ordinarily be settled. The report does not say whether that was Convert Digital's job here.
The contract itself is the third. Kennedy says she "wasn't allowed to get out of the contract," but the report does not identify the counterparty, the length of the term, the fees or the exit conditions.
The fourth concerns the numbers. The 30% fall is Kennedy's estimate, given without a baseline or a time window, and the report does not say whether it covered online sales only or the whole business.
The fifth is the legal position. Adobe cited "legal reasons" for declining to comment, and 7NEWS says mediation failed, but the report does not say which parties took part, whether proceedings have been filed or in which jurisdiction.
The last is the company's status. The report says Adorn would close the day after the video was published. On November 9, 2026, Adorn's website, which runs on Shopify, was still online with a banner appealing for new customers to help save the business and referring to the Channel 7 coverage. Whether a formal insolvency process has started is not stated. Adorn's own founder page dates the company to 2008, while Adobe's case study and B&T give 2009.
A separate case: Adobe's $150 million settlement
The report places the Adorn dispute alongside Adobe's settlement with the US government. "The U.S. government sued Adobe in June 2024 over their termination fees and subscription cancellation policies," the narrator says. "This year it reached a $150 million settlement denying any wrongdoing."
Those facts check out, but the case concerned something different. The Department of Justice, acting on a referral from the Federal Trade Commission, sued Adobe in June 2024, alleging that the company steered customers into its "annual, paid monthly" plan without clearly disclosing an early termination fee of up to 50% of the remaining payments, and made cancellation difficult. The complaint was brought under the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act, the US law that governs online negative option billing, and also named Adobe executives Maninder Sawhney and David Wadhwani. In July 2024, Adobe responded to the amended complaint by saying the fee accounted for less than 0.5% of its total revenue.
On March 13, 2026, the Justice Department announced that it had filed a proposed stipulated order to resolve the case against Adobe and the two employees. According to the department, Adobe would pay $75 million in civil penalties and offer customers $75 million in free services, would have to disclose any early termination fee and how it is calculated before enrolment, remind customers before converting free trials longer than seven days into paid plans carrying such a fee, and provide easy ways to cancel. Adobe said in a statement reported by PetaPixel that it disagreed with the government's claims and denied any wrongdoing.
That case was about consumer subscriptions to software such as Photoshop and Acrobat. It did not involve Adobe Commerce or contracts with merchants, and nothing in the 7NEWS report connects the two matters beyond placing them side by side. The distinction matters for business customers more generally. When the FTC and eight states sued restaurant software company Toast in October 2026 over fees including a $150-per-remaining-month termination charge, Toast argued that the consumer subscription law does not apply to negotiated business contracts. Adorn's agreement, whatever its terms, was a business contract.
Adobe is large by any measure. When the company said in March 2026 that chief executive Shantanu Narayen would step down once a successor is named, PPC Land reported revenue exceeding $25 billion and more than 30,000 employees. Adorn, at its peak, turned over six million dollars a year.
Shopify, the second platform
Kennedy's eventual move was to Shopify, the platform that now runs the Adorn website. The company that Adorn turned to is itself growing quickly: Shopify reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $3.742 billion, up 32%, on gross merchandise volume of $119.1 billion. The report does not say how sales performed after the second migration, only that it came "too late."
Why this matters for the marketing community
Most coverage of e-commerce platforms focuses on features, licence costs and integrations. The Adorn account, whatever its final allocation of blame, points to a different exposure: the dependency between a paid media budget and the website that receives the clicks.
Adorn was not a large advertiser by global standards, yet about a million dollars a year went to two Meta platforms, according to Kennedy. Delivery systems on those platforms learn from conversions. Meta said in October that ad sets with fewer than about 50 weekly conversions cost about 28% more per purchase in its own analysis, without publishing a method. A storefront that converts fewer visitors, or stops reporting conversions correctly, sends fewer of those signals back to the campaigns that depend on them.
The case also shows how decisions about martech for a small brand can carry enterprise-scale consequences. A platform contract, a third-party build and a fixed term can tie up a business for years, and the cost of a failed migration falls on revenue first and on the advertising budget second, because the ads keep running while the site underperforms.
Finally, the report illustrates the limits of vendor projections. 7NEWS says Adobe quoted revenue increases of between 34 and 94 percent; Adobe's published IDC study cited 29% higher platform revenue. The report offers no way to test either projection, or the 30% decline Kennedy describes, and with mediation over and Adobe declining to comment, the public record may stay that thin.
Timeline
- 2008 or 2009: Briony Kennedy founds Adorn Cosmetics in Melbourne (Adorn's site says 2008; Adobe's case study and B&T say 2009). The company uses an open-source version of Magento from its launch, according to B&T.
- May 2018: Adobe agrees to acquire Magento for $1.68 billion.
- September 29, 2021: B&T reports that Adorn is upgrading to Adobe Commerce; Adobe publishes an undated case study on the project.
- December 2021: Adobe's Australian site lists an IDC study, sponsored by Adobe, reporting 29% higher platform revenue for Adobe Commerce users.
- June 17, 2024: The Department of Justice sues Adobe on behalf of the FTC over early termination fees and cancellation practices.
- July 25, 2024: Adobe responds to the amended complaint, saying the fee is less than 0.5% of revenue.
- November 7, 2025: A lazy loading change is linked to a 20% traffic drop at an SEO agency's client.
- March 12, 2026: Adobe says Shantanu Narayen will step down as chief executive once a successor is named.
- March 13, 2026: The Justice Department files a proposed stipulated order under which Adobe pays $75 million in civil penalties and offers $75 million in free services.
- April 27, 2026: Shopify publishes data linking each 100 milliseconds of slower loading to about 3.5% lower conversion.
- June 17, 2026: Google updates its site move guide to cover www and non-www variants.
- October 21, 2026: Meta says ad sets under 50 weekly conversions cost 28% more per purchase.
- October 29, 2026: The FTC and eight states sue Toast; Toast argues the consumer subscription law does not cover business contracts.
- November 3, 2026: Shopify reports third-quarter revenue of $3.742 billion, up 32%.
- November 8, 2026: 7NEWS Australia publishes "Cosmetics empire crumbles after Adobe website disaster" on YouTube; Adobe declines to comment and the report says mediation has failed.
- November 9, 2026: The day the report said Adorn would close; the company's Shopify website remains online with an appeal for customers.

Summary
Who: Briony Kennedy, founder of Melbourne skincare company Adorn Cosmetics; Adobe, whose e-commerce platform Adorn adopted; Convert Digital, the local agency 7NEWS says implemented the change; and 7NEWS Australia, which reported the story.
What: Kennedy told 7NEWS that sales fell by about 30% as soon as the new Adobe-based website launched, that Facebook and Instagram ads costing about one million dollars a year stopped linking back to the site, and that she could not leave the contract. Adorn moved to Shopify, laid off staff and, according to the report, faces closure while Kennedy faces bankruptcy. Adobe declined to comment for legal reasons, and mediation failed.
When: 7NEWS published the report on November 8, 2026. Public material shows Adorn announced its upgrade to Adobe Commerce in September 2021. Adobe's separate $150 million settlement with the US Justice Department was announced on March 13, 2026.
Where: Melbourne, Australia, with Adobe headquartered in the United States.
Why: The case shows how a website platform change can cut off the return on a paid advertising budget, and how much remains unknown when only one party speaks: the role of the implementing agency, the contract terms, the source of the revenue projections and the technical cause of the broken ad links are all unaddressed in the report.
